opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is in where designers spend their attention. Much of chip design today goes into painstaking optimization: squeezing a few percent out of a circuit's area or power, finding a cleaner way to implement an arithmetic unit, tuning things under very tight constraints. Those problems are well specified. You can write down what "better" means and check whether a candidate is correct. That's exactly the regime where something like AlphaEvolve does well. It proposes changes to the actual code or hardware description, evaluates them automatically, keeps what works, and iterates.

We saw an early glimpse of this when AlphaEvolve suggested a rewrite of part of an arithmetic circuit that removed unnecessary bits. The change still had to be verified for functional correctness, and it went through the normal review process with the hardware engineers. That combination matters to me. The system proposes something in the language the designers already use, so they can read it, understand it, and decide whether to trust it. It isn't a black box handing over a mysterious layout.

So my expectation is that chip designers will move up a level. Less time hand-tuning individual blocks, more time on the questions that are hard to formalize. What should the architecture be? What workloads are we really designing for? What are the right objectives and constraints to hand to a system like this? Defining the evaluation function becomes a core skill, because the system will optimize whatever you ask it to, including your mistakes.

There's also a nice feedback loop. Better chips make training and running these models more efficient, and more efficient models get better at helping design the next generation of hardware. That's part of why we care so much about this area. It isn't just one application among many. It speeds up the whole stack.

I don't think this replaces the expertise of hardware engineers. Their intuition is what lets them ask good questions and judge the answers. What changes is the size of the search they can effectively explore. Ideas that were too tedious or too expensive to try by hand suddenly become things you can test overnight. And I think that will change which problems people consider worth attacking at all.

r001.rationale: The response says the expanded search makes previously too tedious or expensive ideas testable, changing which problems designers consider worth attacking.

r002.rationale: It says designers will move toward defining architectures, workloads, objectives, constraints, and evaluation functions for AlphaEvolve to optimize.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it won't so much remove problems from the chip designer's plate as it will change which layer of the problem they spend their time on.

If you look at what AlphaEvolve actually did on the TPU work, it found a small simplification in an arithmetic circuit inside the matrix multiplication unit, written in Verilog, that engineers could verify was correct and actually ship. That's a modest-sounding thing, but what matters is how it got there. It wasn't someone sitting down and reasoning about that circuit for weeks. It was a system proposing candidate changes, having them evaluated automatically against functional correctness and against the metrics the team cares about, and iterating on the ones that looked promising. The human role shifted from writing the solution to specifying what a good solution looks like and then validating what came back.

So I think the first change is that designers increasingly become the people who define the search problem well. What is the objective? What are the constraints that are non-negotiable, like correctness and timing, versus the ones you're willing to trade, like area or power? How do you build an evaluator that is fast enough to run thousands of times and still faithful to what you'll measure on silicon? That evaluator design is going to be where a lot of the engineering judgment lives, because the system is only as good as the signal you give it.

The second change is in the kind of optimization people attempt at all. There are a lot of places in a chip where a designer knows there's probably a better micro-architecture or a tighter piece of logic, but the search space is big and the payoff of any single one is small, so it never gets prioritized. When exploring that space becomes cheap, those long-tail opportunities become worth going after, and they compound. I expect we'll see teams revisit parts of a design they considered done.

And the third thing, which I find most interesting, is the feedback loop between the model and the hardware. We used AlphaEvolve to improve the kernels that train Gemini, and we used it on the hardware that runs those kernels. The more you close that loop, the more co-design becomes a practical workflow rather than an aspiration. Designers start to ask not just how to build a better chip, but how to make the chip, the compiler, and the model move together.

I do want to be careful not to overclaim. These systems are good at problems where you can check an answer automatically. A large part of chip design is still judgment about things that are hard to score, and verification remains the bottleneck it has always been. So I'd describe it less as replacing chip designers and more as giving them a very fast, very tireless collaborator for the parts of the job that are search, so they can spend more of their own attention on the parts that are taste.

r001.rationale: The response says cheaper search makes long-tail opportunities worth pursuing, but it does not connect problem selection to AlphaEvolve solving problems beyond human capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says designers will define the search problem, including its objectives, constraints, and evaluator, which communicates that stronger optimization systems enable more sophisticated problem formulation.

astra-6.text:
I think it expands the space of designs that people can explore. In chip design, you’re balancing many objectives—performance, power consumption, area—and even a small improvement can be very valuable when it’s deployed at scale.

AlphaEvolve can help search for those improvements. If you can express a design problem in code and reliably evaluate a proposed change, you can set up a loop where the system generates candidates, tests them, and builds on the ones that work. It may find solutions that a designer wouldn’t naturally think to try.

That shifts some of the designer’s work toward deciding what to optimize, specifying the constraints, and making sure the evaluation captures what actually matters. The exciting possibility is that ideas that were previously too expensive to explore become practical to investigate. Human judgment remains essential, but the search space you can tackle becomes much larger.

r001.rationale: It mentions deciding what to optimize, but does not identify which problems are worth solving as a central question raised by AlphaEvolve solving beyond human capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says AlphaEvolve can search for improvements across objectives and shifts designers toward deciding what to optimize and specifying constraints, conveying that the system enables more sophisticated optimization problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could change both how designers solve problems and which problems they’re willing to tackle. Chip design involves an enormous space of possible choices, and engineers have limited time to explore it. A system like AlphaEvolve can help search that space, propose changes, and test them against concrete measures of performance and correctness.

That could let designers revisit assumptions that have become standard practice. Is this particular constraint fundamental, or is it simply a choice we’ve carried forward? Can we find a better trade-off between power, area, and speed?

The engineer still has to define the problem and decide what matters. But if exploring alternatives becomes cheaper, they can spend more time on ambitious questions that previously seemed too expensive to investigate.

r001.rationale: The response says designers may tackle more ambitious questions, but does not connect this to AlphaEvolve solving problems beyond human capabilities or identify that as the central question.

r002.rationale: It describes cheaper exploration and revisiting assumptions, but does not state that advanced optimization systems let designers formulate more sophisticated optimization problems.
